title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
claim: A frozen model is adapted by learning a binary keep-or-delete mask, annealed from a soft sigmoid to a hard threshold, with no new weight values.
layout: 4 panels, left-to-right, operator symbols and arrows between them, sigmoid plot in the middle
description: A single horizontal strip reads left to right. First panel: a 4x4 grid of gray squares labeled 'Pretrained W' with a snowflake icon, meaning frozen. A circled-dot (Hadamard product) symbol links it to the second panel, 'Gate logits G' with a flame icon, meaning trainable. That panel is a 4x4 grid of blue squares of varying shades, with a few red ones. A legend marks blue as kept and red as deleted. An arrow leads to a plot of sigma(alpha G) with alpha increasing. Gray curves sharpen into a step function at G=0. The background is pink on the left and blue on the right. A second arrow labeled alpha→∞ leads to 'Deployed W ⊙ 1[G>0]'. That panel repeats the gray grid with two red dotted boxes containing X marks, and the caption 'adapter: 1 bit / weight'. The eye goes first to the colored logit grid and the sigmoid plot.
caption: \looseness=-10000 \textbf{\ourmethodit{} learns which pretrained weights to delete and writes no new values.} The pretrained weights $W$ stay frozen, and each is paired with a trainable logit in $G$, the only parameters that post-training updates. During training, each weight is multiplied by $\sigma(\alpha G)$, a smooth mask between $0$ and $1$. The sharpness $\alpha$ rises over training until the sigmoid becomes a hard threshold at $G = 0$. At deployment, weights with positive logits (blue) keep their pretrained values and weights with negative logits (red) are set to zero (crossed out), so the trained adapter is one bit per weight.
abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.
